sections.heading: What is ibuprofen used for?
sections.body: Ibuprofen is a painkiller that also treats inflammation. Inflammation is the swelling and soreness that can come with an injury or a joint problem. It belongs to a group of medicines called non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or NSAIDs. Ibuprofen comes as tablets, capsules, granules and liquid that are swallowed, and as gel, mousse or spray that is applied to the skin. The NHS describes it as an everyday painkiller for back pain, period pain, toothache and cold or flu symptoms, and says it also treats inflammation such as sprains, strains and arthritis pain. The NHS says it does not usually work well for nerve pain, and that a doctor may need to prescribe a different medicine when pain is related to the nerves. The NHS compares ibuprofen with other painkillers, including paracetamol, aspirin and co-codamol, which combines paracetamol with low-dose codeine. It says ibuprofen can cause more side effects than paracetamol, and it has a separate page on who can and cannot take ibuprofen.

sections.heading: How does ibuprofen work?
sections.body: The NHS says ibuprofen works by lowering the amount of certain hormones in the body that cause pain and swelling. With less of these chemicals, there is less pain and less swelling. A hospital leaflet explains that tissue injury prompts the body to make chemicals called prostaglandins, which are involved in pain and inflammation, and that NSAIDs reduce their amount. A medical reference says ibuprofen blocks enzymes called cyclo-oxygenase, which reduces the making of prostaglandins and similar chemicals. The same reference says these chemicals also help to protect the stomach lining and to maintain blood flow to the kidneys, so stomach and kidney side effects trace back to the same pathway. The NHS says swallowed forms start to work soon after they are taken, while skin products take a day or two to start working. It says some people take ibuprofen for many years when a doctor prescribes it. Ulcers are a risk with long-term use or large amounts, and a doctor may prescribe a stomach-protecting medicine for people at risk. The NHS also says that someone already taking ibuprofen by mouth regularly gets no extra benefit from also using the gel.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of ibuprofen?
sections.body: The NHS lists indigestion and stomach aches, feeling sick, headaches, a rash, dizziness, and diarrhoea or constipation among the common side effects. If dizziness happens, the NHS advises against driving or riding a bike until it passes. The NHS says the gel may make the eyes, mouth, lips, nose or genital area sore if it gets there. Rarer serious effects include bleeding in the stomach and a serious allergic reaction called anaphylaxis. MedlinePlus, a US source, says ibuprofen can cause ulcers, bleeding or holes in the oesophagus, stomach or intestine, and that these can happen without warning symptoms. The NHS lists black poo, which can be a sign of bleeding in the stomach, as a serious side effect. It says swollen ankles or blood in the urine are reasons to contact a doctor or NHS 111. The NHS says swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or fast or difficult breathing, is a reason to call 999. MedlinePlus says NSAIDs such as ibuprofen may raise the risk of a heart attack or stroke, and that the risk is higher with long-term or high-amount use.

sections.heading: Taking ibuprofen with food, alcohol or other medicines
sections.body: The NHS says tablets, capsules, granules and liquid can be taken with food or milk, which makes an upset stomach less likely. On alcohol, the NHS says it is usually not a problem to drink some, but drinking too much can irritate the stomach when ibuprofen is swallowed. MedlinePlus says heavy alcohol use is one of the things that raises the risk of ulcers and bleeding with ibuprofen. Some UK patient leaflets go further and advise avoiding alcohol, because it may add to side effects in the stomach, intestines or nervous system. The NHS says ibuprofen should not be combined with other NSAIDs such as naproxen or aspirin, because that raises the risk of serious effects such as stomach ulcers. Medical references describe several medicines that interact with ibuprofen. Ibuprofen can reduce the blood-pressure-lowering effect of ACE inhibitors and may weaken the effect of diuretics. Taking it with warfarin raises the risk of serious bleeding in the stomach and gut, and it can raise the level of lithium in the blood.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with ibuprofen?
sections.body: The NHS lists reasons not to take ibuprofen, including a past allergic reaction to aspirin or another NSAID, pregnancy, a history of stomach ulcers, and severe heart, kidney or liver failure. MedlinePlus says the risk of ulcers and bleeding is higher with long-term use, older age, poor health, smoking or heavy alcohol use. Asthma, hay fever and allergies are listed by the NHS as conditions to check with a doctor or pharmacist about first. MedlinePlus says people who have recently had a heart attack should not take ibuprofen unless a doctor directs it. Some UK leaflets list an increased tendency to bleed as a reason not to take it. UK leaflets say it should not be taken in the last three months of pregnancy, because it could harm the unborn baby or cause problems at delivery, and may cause labour to be later or longer than expected.

faqs.q: Can ibuprofen be taken on an empty stomach?
faqs.a: The NHS says tablets, capsules, granules and liquid can be taken with food or milk, which makes an upset stomach less likely. Ulcers are a risk with long-term use or large amounts, and a doctor may prescribe a stomach-protecting medicine for people at risk. The NHS lists black poo as a serious side effect, and swollen ankles or blood in the urine as reasons to contact a doctor or NHS 111.

faqs.q: How long does ibuprofen take to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says swallowed forms start to work soon after they are taken, while gel and other skin products take a day or two. It does not usually work well for nerve pain. If pharmacy painkillers do not work, the NHS says a doctor may prescribe a stronger painkiller or suggest another treatment, such as exercise or physiotherapy.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking ibuprofen?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is usually not a problem to drink some alcohol with ibuprofen, but drinking too much can irritate the stomach when it is swallowed. MedlinePlus says heavy alcohol use raises the risk of ulcers and bleeding. Some UK patient leaflets advise avoiding alcohol, because it may add to side effects in the stomach, intestines or nervous system.

faqs.q: Can ibuprofen be taken in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS lists pregnancy as a reason not to take ibuprofen. UK leaflets say it should not be taken in the last three months of pregnancy, because it could harm the unborn baby or cause problems at delivery. They also say it should generally not be used in the first six months unless a doctor judges it necessary.
